memoryText: But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD.
readingInstruction: Today there is no new reading. The week you have just completed was a hinge week, closing Unit 1 and opening Unit 2. Take time today to let both arcs settle. The God who created in the beginning is the same God who showed grace to Noah.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Genesis 6:8 is the first appearance of the word “grace” (Hebrew hen) in the Bible. The conjunction “But” is everything. The verses surrounding it describe the worst assessment of humanity in the Old Testament, “every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually” (6:5). And then: BUT Noah found favor.

Notice what the verse does not say. It does not say Noah earned favor. It does not say Noah deserved favor. It says he FOUND it, and grace, by definition, is what is found, not what is achieved.

Say the verse with the conjunction loud in your mind. The “But” is the gospel’s word. In a world of judgment, there is a “But.” In a heart of rebellion, there is a “But.” That “But” is the difference between being lost with the world and being saved by grace.
weekInReview:
This week was a pivot. You finished Unit 1 with Psalm 65, David’s integrated meditation on creation and atonement, and the Unit 1 Review, anchored on Genesis 1:1. Then Unit 2 began. You met Cain, the first murderer, and heard God’s warning that “sin is crouching at the door.” You walked through the genealogy of Genesis 5, with the repeated phrase “and he died” broken only by Enoch, who walked with God. You met Noah in Genesis 6 and learned that grace is what is found, not earned. And you began the flood narrative in Genesis 7, watching judgment fall on a world that had refused God’s patience.

The arc of the week is the arc of the gospel itself. Sin spreads. Judgment comes. But Noah, and ultimately Christ, finds favor with God, and through that one, others are preserved.
reflectionQuestions: Where do you see God’s patience and his judgment held together in this week’s readings? The first half of the week celebrated creation; the second half showed the spread of sin and the coming of judgment. Both are true at once. Where do you most need to remember God’s patience this week? Where do you most need to remember his judgment?

How does Noah’s grace prefigure the grace you have received in Christ? Noah did not deserve to be saved any more than the people who drowned. He found favor. Through one righteous man, his family was preserved through the flood. Through one righteous Man, you have been preserved through the judgment your sin deserved. Sit with this. What does it mean that you have found grace, not earned it?

What does it look like for you, today, to “walk with God” as Enoch did? The phrase appears only twice about individuals in the Old Testament, Enoch and Noah. Both lived in cultures sliding into wickedness. Both were marked by a different kind of life. What would it take for that to be true of you?
prayerPrompts: Thank God for the grace behind every “But God” in your own story.
Ask him to help you walk humbly and gratefully this week in a world that does not walk with him.
Rest in the favor he has shown you in Christ.
